Inventory improvement in developing countries should prioritize routine core data collection, transparent documentation, targeted sectoral and facility-level detail, careful evaluation of non-state data products and task-specific use of advanced methods. Sustained institutional capacity and long-term data stewardship are therefore central to closing the inventory gaps.

title: Traffic and combustion emission controls leave cooking as a dominant local source of primary PM1 in megacities
abstract: Megacities frequently suffer from poor air quality, with PM 2.5 concentrations routinely exceeding WHO guidelines and elevating the risk of cardiovascular and respiratory disease. Air quality legislation typically targets primary emissions from traffic, a dominant urban source of PM₂.₅. Here, we present direct, chemically resolved quantification of PM₁ emissions from three contrasting megacity neighbourhoods—London, Beijing and Delhi—revealing the magnitude and diversity of urban sources by applying a novel source attribution approach to eddy-covariance flux measurements using aerosol mass spectrometry. In Delhi, traffic and combustion dominate primary PM₁ emissions. In contrast, cooking is the largest source during mealtimes in London and Beijing, contributing up to 83% of midday emissions and 87% in the early evening in London, and up to 61% and 76%, respectively, in Beijing. These findings suggest that air quality legislation in London and Beijing has effectively reduced non-refractory transport and combustion emissions, allowing cooking to emerge as the largest local source of primary non-refractory PM₁. Although cooking is not included in national, European or global emission inventories, recent estimates from the London Atmospheric Emissions Inventory align well with our observations. Together, these results show that the sources dominating primary non-refractory PM₁ emissions differ from those controlling ambient PM 1 mass. Although cooking is now the leading primary source in London and Beijing, further reductions in urban PM₁ will depend on mitigating secondary formation processes.

title: The dryness control of MJO emergence
abstract: Despite decades of researches into the Madden–Julian Oscillation (MJO) dynamics, the mechanisms of the MJO initiation from the eastern Africa–western Indian Ocean remain a major barrier to subseasonal predictions. Here, we identify a unique controlling effect on the MJO emergence by the preceding suppressed convection over the Indian Ocean (IOSC) and western Pacific (WPSC) that likely originates from Southern-hemisphere wave trains. A topographic pathway is tactfully revealed: East-African highlands force southerly transitions via the mechanical blocking of equatorial westerlies responding to an anomalous convective pattern. Consequently, moist air is advected from equatorial Africa to fuel the MJO emergence. Ensemble high-resolution simulations confirm this hidden topographic link. Moreover, the IOSC flattens the background moisture gradient over the Indian Ocean, while the WPSC introduces anomalous westerlies due to its westward propagation, both lowering the efficiency of the horizontal moisture advection in initiating the MJO. These findings advance our understanding of MJO genesis pathways from perspectives of topographic-link and moisture sources over equatorial Africa.

title: Exceptionally high temperatures in Armenia in 2023: orographic effects, snowpack response and synoptic drivers
abstract: Climate conditions in 2023 were exceptionally warm globally. Armenia experienced exceptionally high temperatures in March, November and December 2023, resulting in an extremely low mountain snowpack. Advective processes associated with meridional (in March) and zonal (November-December) flows were dominant large-scale factors producing strong positive temperature anomalies across Armenia. Mountain topography both dampened and enhanced positive temperature anomalies through formation of nocturnal cold-air pooling and stronger daytime radiative heating, respectively.

title: Monsoon-driven dry-wet seasonal contrast reveals mitigation opportunity for methane emissions in South Asia
abstract: South Asia is a global methane (CH 4 ) hotspot with strong monsoon-driven seasonality, yet wet-season emissions remain poorly constrained due to persistent cloudiness. Here we quantify dry- and wet-season methane emissions separately over South Asia during 2019–2024 using TROPOMI-constrained analytical inversions. By leveraging satellite observations from downwind regions, we are able to effectively constrain wet-season emissions despite sparse coverage. Anthropogenic sources dominate the regional total, accounting for 77.2% (28.8 Tg a −1 ; interannual range: 25.3–30.9 Tg a⁻¹), with major contributions from livestock (35.0% (32.9%–36.0%)), rice cultivation (21.8% (20.4%–23.1%)), and waste management (13.8% (12.4%–14.5%)). Six-year mean wet-season emissions (49.9(44.6–53.4) Tg a -1 ) are nearly twice dry season emissions (28.2(23.8–33.6) Tg a −1 ), driven by wetlands (5.5×), rice (2.6×), waste management (1.2×), and fossil fuels (1.2×); seasonality in waste and fossil fuels emissions is however missing from current inventories. Furthermore, latest national reports underestimate India’s methane emissions partly by neglecting seasonal variability. Despite much larger wet-season emissions, dry-season livestock and waste, unexpectedly, dominate interannual variability, likely indicating sensitivity to climate anomalies and potential implications for climate-resilient mitigation. South Asia contributed substantially to global methane surge in 2021, but not 2020. Our findings underpin previously-overlooked mitigation priorities that vary sharply by season.

title: Disentangling the anthropogenic climate change influence on recent hydroclimate whiplash events via multiple nudged model simulations
abstract: Hydroclimate whiplash describes swings between extremely dry and wet conditions. The magnitude and physical drivers of changes in observed whiplash events under global warming remain poorly understood. Here we quantify thermodynamically-driven changes in whiplash intensity for nine high-impact events using the Standardised Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index and a unique multi-model ensemble of wind-nudged storyline simulations. Anthropogenic climate change accounts for 9% (range across events: −2 to 72%) of the observed whiplash intensity on a weighted average across events, with positive contributions for nearly all events according to the multi-model mean, and all models agreeing on the positive contribution for about two-thirds of the events. This climate change contribution is predominantly driven by a non-linear increase in potential evapotranspiration, which strengthens drying more during the dry than the wet phase. Model uncertainty on the magnitude of the climate change contribution is substantial, with an inter-model spread of 13% on average across the events. These results highlight a climate change imprint on observed whiplash events and the need for multiple nudged datasets to robustly attribute complex events.

title: Disentangling dynamic and thermodynamic pathways reveals nonlocal winter climate responses to historical land use and land cover change
abstract: Historical land use and land cover change (LULCC) can influence both nearby and distant climates through land–atmosphere interactions, yet its non-local climatic impacts remain poorly constrained. One possible explanation is that previous studies conflated non-local effects arising from distinct physical processes. Here we used CMIP6 models to separate the influences of large-scale circulation, thermodynamic advection, and local surface energy balance in winter surface air temperature responses to historical LULCC. We show that circulation-induced changes generate weak but significant warming over the Canada–Greenland region, with negligible signals elsewhere. After removing this dynamic component, a widespread and robust thermodynamic cooling signal emerges in the mid-latitudes due to advection, with magnitudes of ~0.3 K across hotspot regions and local areas cooling up to 1 K. Local energy contributions are smaller, mainly linked to albedo and downward longwave radiation changes. This process-based attribution significantly reduces inter-model spread, advances the mechanistic understanding of land–atmosphere interactions, and highlights the importance of considering non-local climate effects in assessments of land-use change and climate mitigation strategies.

title: Skillful subseasonal-to-seasonal ensemble forecasting with a multi-sphere coupled probabilistic model
abstract: Accurate subseasonal-to-seasonal (S2S) prediction is critical for disaster mitigation under accelerating climate change, yet remains challenging due to complex multi-sphere interactions and intrinsic atmospheric uncertainty. Here we present TianXing-S2S, a multi-sphere coupled probabilistic deep learning model for global S2S ensemble forecasting. TianXing-S2S first encodes diverse multi-sphere predictors into a compact latent space, then employs a diffusion model to generate daily ensemble forecasts. A novel coupling module based on optimal transport (OT) is incorporated in the denoiser to optimize the interactions between atmospheric and multi-sphere boundary conditions. Across key atmospheric variables, TianXing-S2S outperforms both the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) S2S system and FuXi-S2S in 45-day daily-mean ensemble forecasts at 1.5° × 1.5° resolution. Our model improves the prediction of extreme events including heat waves and anomalous precipitation, with multi-sphere coupling identified as a key contributor. Furthermore, we demonstrate that TianXing-S2S can generate stable rollout forecasts up to 180 days, suggesting its potential as a useful framework for probabilistic S2S prediction under a changing climate.

title: Generative assimilation and prediction for weather and climate
abstract: Machine learning models have shown great success in predicting weather up to two weeks ahead, outperforming process-based benchmarks 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 . However, most existing approaches do not fully integrate data assimilation into the prediction workflow 6 , 7 , and often suffer from error accumulation in autoregressive computation, limiting their applicability to predictions beyond the medium range 8 and climate projections 9 . We introduce Generative Assimilation and Prediction (GAP), a unified deep generative framework that connects data assimilation, weather forecasting, and climate simulation through a shared probabilistic representation of atmospheric states. GAP learns the climatological distribution from reanalysis data, and adapts it to different tasks by incorporating observational, predictive, and forcing constraints. Evaluated across a range of weather-climate tasks, GAP produces probabilistic weather forecasts competitive with leading forecasting systems, using its own assimilated initial states derived from 5% synthetic perfect observations, with particular skill in capturing extreme events such as atmospheric rivers, heatwaves and the Madden-Julian Oscillation. At seasonal timescales, GAP shows promising predictive skill when constrained by oceanic boundary forcing. Moreover, GAP supports stable millennial-scale climate simulations that reproduce atmospheric variability from daily weather fluctuations to decadal oscillations. These results suggest that generative modeling of the climatological distribution offers a viable foundation for seamless weather and climate prediction, thereby opening a path toward integrated, observation-to-climate workflows.

title: Why the least nocturnal convection initiation yields the most upscale convective growth over South China
abstract: Upscale convective growth (UCG) is the key process forming mesoscale convective systems that dominate warm-season heavy rainfall. A recent decade of South China events shows coastal UCG is misaligned with convection initiation (CI): it peaks at night, when CI is weakest. Nocturnal UCG reflects higher organizational efficiency, not more frequent triggering, despite daytime peak instability and CI. Both contrasts arise from the same boundary-layer wind cycle. By day, opposing sea-breeze and offshore oceanic departure winds yield a weak, narrow coastal convergence band, and northward storm motion carries systems away from it. At night, onshore oceanic departure winds converge with the land breeze, forming a stronger, broader lifting corridor, while the same southerly enhancement reorients the low-level wind maximum, making storm motion zonal and band-aligned. Enhanced coastal lifting and along-band propagation favor nocturnal UCG. Climate-sensitive land-sea thermal contrast and phase-locked oceanic wind anomalies could reshape coastal heavy-rainfall hazards beyond South China.

title: Refined SOA hygroscopicity reduces climate-relevant uncertainties in aerosol liquid water and CCN predictions
abstract: Large uncertainties in atmospheric organic aerosol (OA) hygroscopicity substantially limit the accurate evaluation of aerosol physicochemical evolution, aqueous-phase processing, and aerosol-cloud climatic effects. Traditional retrieval methods generally adopt simplified homogeneous mixing assumptions or oxidation-dependent parameterizations, which largely neglect ambient mixing-state heterogeneity and may cause systematic biases in secondary organic aerosol hygroscopicity ( κ SOA ) estimation. Herein, based on wintertime field observations in Beijing, we develop a mixing state-resolved approach to retrieve size-resolved κ SOA by accounting for the partitioning of aerosol chemical components between hydrophobic and hygroscopic modes. Approximately 93% of the retrieved κ SOA values exceed 0.20, with a campaign average of 0.47 ± 0.20, whereas conventional schemes severely underestimate ambient κ SOA by approximately 50%. Such biases are particularly pronounced for larger particles (>80 nm) with complex mixing transitions. Chemical and mechanistic validations confirm that elevated κ SOA is dominated by highly hygroscopic low-molecular-weight organic acids formed via aqueous acid-catalyzed reactions. Benefiting from the refined κ SOA constraint, our approach substantially improves aerosol liquid water closure ( R 2 = 0.96), reduces low-humidity water-uptake underestimation, and enhances cloud condensation nuclei number concentration prediction accuracy by 3–10%. This study highlights that explicitly resolving aerosol mixing state is critical for narrowing OA hygroscopicity uncertainties and reliably simulating aerosol environmental and climatic effects.

title: Responses of surface radiative balance to wildfires differ across ecosystems
abstract: Wildfires alter land surface albedo and temperature, modulating the radiative budget and climate. Previous studies have predominantly reported enhanced shortwave absorption induced by post-fire surface darkening over forests. Here, using two-decade (2001–2020) satellite observations of wildfires, we show that post-fire summer surface albedo and radiative balance shifts vary significantly across ecosystems. Broadleaf forests and grasslands exhibit a brightening effect, because the exposure of bright soils and rapid vegetation regrowth outweigh the deposition of dark carbonaceous residues. The post-fire surface brightening then amplifies the warming-driven radiative cooling. Conversely, in needleleaf forests, shrublands, and savannas, post-fire surface darkening increases shortwave absorption, yet warming-driven longwave radiative losses remain dominant, leading to net radiative cooling. Surface radiative fluxes exhibit high sensitivity to fire size in mid-to-high latitude regions driven by distinct fire-ecosystem feedbacks. Therefore, the ecosystem heterogeneity must be considered when assessing the effects of wildfires on the surface radiative budget and climate.

title: Global Rossby wave rivers connecting remote wave activity to the East Asian summer monsoon
abstract: We introduce a sink-oriented Rossby wave river (WR) framework that traces remote wave activity along continuous propagation pathways converging toward specific sinks, and use the Li-Yang wave ray flux to diagnose the global WRs converging into the East Asian summer monsoon (EASM) region. At 850 hPa, Southern Hemisphere and pan-tropical pathways dominate and converge near the Philippines; at 500 hPa, low-latitude easterly and midlatitude westerly WRs become comparable in strength; at 200 hPa, WR propagation becomes concentrated along the jet waveguide. Strikingly, the two major 500-hPa WRs undergo nearly head-on confluence, forming a climatological Rossby wave front that closely coincides with the Meiyu front. Vertically, the dominant pathway shifts from the southern monsoon channel below to the northwestern westerly waveguide aloft, with the transition occurring above the Meiyu–Changma–Baiu rainband. This sink-oriented perspective reframes EASM teleconnections as an interconnected global wave-propagation network linking remote Rossby wave sources to regional climate impacts.
